question: An aircraft is said to be "statically stable" about an axis if, when disturbed from equilibrium, it:

options.text: Immediately returns to its original attitude with no further oscillation
Shows an initial tendency to move back toward its original equilibrium condition
Continues to diverge further away from its original equilibrium condition
Remains exactly where the disturbance left it, with no tendency to move either way

explanation: Static stability describes only the initial tendency following a disturbance: a statically stable aircraft's forces and moments initially act to move it back toward equilibrium. Whether it actually gets there smoothly, oscillates, or overshoots is a separate question of dynamic stability.

question: Moving an aircraft's center of gravity further aft, toward the aft limit, generally has what effect on longitudinal stability?

options.text: It increases longitudinal stability, requiring larger elevator inputs
It decreases longitudinal stability, and reduces the elevator authority needed to raise the nose
It has no effect, since longitudinal stability depends only on tailplane area
It changes the aircraft from statically stable in pitch to stable only at low speed

explanation: As the center of gravity moves aft, it moves closer to the aircraft's neutral point, shortening the stabilising moment arm the tailplane can generate. This reduces longitudinal static stability, makes the aircraft more sensitive to elevator input, and — beyond the aft limit — can make it unstable in pitch.

question: The "phugoid" oscillation is best described as:

options.text: A rapid, short-period oscillation in angle of attack with the airspeed remaining almost constant
A long-period oscillation in pitch attitude, airspeed and altitude, occurring at a nearly constant angle of attack
A purely lateral oscillation involving roll and yaw with no change in pitch
An oscillation that only occurs when the aircraft is stalled

explanation: The phugoid is a slow, long-period exchange between kinetic and potential energy: the nose rises and speed falls, then the nose drops and speed rises, repeating over tens of seconds, while angle of attack stays nearly constant throughout. This is distinct from the short-period pitch oscillation, which involves rapid angle-of-attack changes at almost constant speed.

question: The "short-period" pitch oscillation, unlike the phugoid, involves:

options.text: A slow trade between speed and altitude at a constant angle of attack
A rapid change in angle of attack at essentially constant airspeed, usually heavily damped
Only lateral motion, with no pitch change at all
A motion that only occurs below the stalling speed

explanation: The short-period mode is a fast oscillation in angle of attack and pitch rate that occurs over a couple of seconds at essentially constant airspeed, and it is normally strongly damped by the tailplane. It is the mode a pilot excites with a single, brief elevator pulse; the phugoid is the much slower mode that follows afterward.

question: The "neutral point" of an aircraft is the center of gravity position at which:

options.text: Longitudinal static stability is at its maximum
The aircraft has zero longitudinal static stability — moving the CG any further aft would make it unstable
The aircraft cannot be trimmed at all
The elevator has no effect whatsoever

explanation: The neutral point is the theoretical center of gravity position at which the whole aircraft's pitching moment no longer changes with angle of attack — zero static stability. A center of gravity ahead of it gives positive stability; one behind it gives negative stability (instability), which is why the aft CG limit is always set forward of the neutral point.

question: The "static margin" is defined as the distance between:

options.text: The wingtip and the fuselage centerline
The center of gravity and the neutral point, expressed as a percentage of the mean aerodynamic chord — a larger margin means greater longitudinal stability
The leading edge and the trailing edge
The aerodynamic center and the wingtip

explanation: Static margin measures how far ahead of the neutral point the center of gravity sits, normalised to the mean aerodynamic chord so it can be compared between different aircraft sizes. The larger this margin, the more strongly the aircraft resists a pitch disturbance.

question: "Stick-free" longitudinal stability differs from "stick-fixed" stability in that it accounts for:

options.text: The aircraft flying with no pilot at all
The elevator being free to float aerodynamically, with the controls released, rather than held rigidly in place — which can change the effective stability
Only ground handling, not flight
The landing gear position

explanation: "Stick-fixed" stability assumes the elevator is locked at a set position; "stick-free" stability instead lets it float freely and align itself aerodynamically with the local airflow, which changes the tailplane's effective contribution and can make stick-free stability somewhat different — usually slightly less — than stick-fixed stability.

question: In trimmed, straight-and-level flight, a conventional horizontal tailplane typically produces a small download. This download exists mainly to:

options.text: Increase total lift beyond what the wing alone produces
Balance the wing's own nose-down pitching moment, produced by its camber, about the center of gravity
Reduce induced drag
Increase the critical Mach number

explanation: A cambered wing alone produces a nose-down pitching moment about its aerodynamic center. To balance the whole aircraft in trimmed flight, the tailplane usually generates a small download at a moment arm from the center of gravity, and that download's own moment offsets the wing's nose-down tendency.

question: Moving the center of gravity forward, within limits, generally:

options.text: Increases longitudinal stability but requires more elevator (up-elevator) authority to reach a high angle of attack, such as for a landing flare
Decreases longitudinal stability and reduces elevator authority
Has no effect on stability or elevator requirements
Makes the aircraft impossible to trim

explanation: A forward CG lengthens the tailplane's stabilising moment arm and improves stability, but it also means the tailplane must work harder — deflecting the elevator further — to generate enough nose-up moment to reach a given angle of attack, which is why a very forward CG can, in the extreme, threaten enough elevator authority to flare for landing.

question: The horizontal tailplane on many aircraft is set at a slightly lower angle of incidence than the wing — a difference sometimes called "longitudinal dihedral". Its main purpose is to help ensure that:

options.text: The tailplane always stalls before the wing
The wing stalls before the tailplane loses effectiveness, since the tailplane operates at a correspondingly lower local angle of attack for a given aircraft attitude
The tailplane produces more lift than the wing
The tailplane always stalls at the same time as the wing

explanation: By setting the tailplane at a lower incidence than the wing, the tailplane operates at a correspondingly lower angle of attack for any given aircraft attitude — helping to ensure the main wing reaches its own critical angle of attack and stalls before the tailplane could lose effectiveness first, which would be far more dangerous.

question: "Stability" and "controllability" are related but distinct design requirements, in that a highly stable aircraft can end up:

options.text: Sluggish and resistant to change, making it less responsive to deliberate control inputs — the two properties can trade off against each other
Automatically more manoeuvrable as a direct result of being more stable
Identical in every respect to a highly controllable one
Unable to be trimmed at all

explanation: Stability describes an aircraft's tendency to resist and recover from a disturbance on its own; controllability describes how readily a pilot can deliberately change its flight condition. A very stable aircraft resists disturbances well but can also resist a pilot's own deliberate inputs, making the two genuinely separate — sometimes conflicting — design goals.

question: An engine thrust line positioned above the center of gravity tends to produce, when power is increased:

options.text: A nose-down pitching moment
A nose-up pitching moment
No pitching moment at all, regardless of thrust line position
A rolling moment only

explanation: Thrust acting along a line above the center of gravity creates a moment that pitches the nose down as power is increased, since the thrust vector's line of action passes above, rather than through, the point the aircraft actually rotates about — the opposite effect to a thrust line below the CG, which pitches the nose up with increasing power.

question: A T-tail's elevator often provides particularly strong pitch authority at high angle of attack mainly because the tailplane, mounted atop the fin, is:

options.text: Positioned clear of the wing's downwash, letting it operate in relatively undisturbed airflow across a wider range of aircraft attitudes
Always smaller in area than a conventional low-mounted tailplane
Unable to move at all
Directly connected to the wing's own flaps

explanation: Mounted well above the fuselage and wing, a T-tail's tailplane largely avoids the wing's downwash field that a conventional low-set tailplane sits within, letting it operate in cleaner, more predictable airflow across a wider range of attitudes — part of why T-tails are often praised for strong elevator authority, right up until the wing's wake can blanket them entirely at a high enough angle of attack.

question: Even before reaching a full tailplane stall, ice accumulation on the tailplane's leading edge can:

options.text: Reduce the tailplane's lift (or download) margin and effectiveness, eroding longitudinal stability well before any dramatic event occurs
Have absolutely no effect until the tailplane fully stalls
Always increase the tailplane's effectiveness
Only affect the wing, never the tailplane's own performance

explanation: Well short of a full tailplane stall, ice on the tailplane's leading edge already degrades its aerodynamic performance and reduces its margin before losing effectiveness — a progressive erosion of longitudinal stability, not simply a binary condition that is fine until it suddenly is not.

question: On a twin-engine aircraft with wing-mounted engines, losing one engine can have a secondary effect on longitudinal control because:

options.text: The loss of that engine's slipstream over the tail can locally reduce elevator effectiveness, on top of the more obvious yaw and roll effects of asymmetric thrust
Engine failure has no effect on the tailplane in any way
It always increases elevator effectiveness
It only affects rudder, never elevator

explanation: Beyond the well-known yawing and rolling consequences of asymmetric thrust, losing an engine also removes that engine's own contribution to slipstream-energised airflow reaching the tail, which can measurably affect elevator effectiveness alongside the primary directional control challenge.

question: An aircraft's center of gravity can shift rearward during a flight mainly due to:

options.text: Fuel being burned from tanks positioned ahead of the CG, or passengers/cargo shifting aft
The aircraft's structure permanently changing shape
Increasing altitude alone, with no other cause
Airspeed changes alone

explanation: As fuel is consumed from tanks that sit ahead of the center of gravity, or if cargo or passenger weight shifts aft during flight, the overall center of gravity moves progressively rearward — which is why loading calculations must account not just for the CG at takeoff, but for how it will move over the course of the flight.

question: "Trim drag" refers to the extra drag produced because:

options.text: Balancing the aircraft in trimmed flight usually requires a small deflection of the elevator (or tailplane), which itself adds a small amount of drag
Trimming the aircraft always eliminates all drag
Trim drag only exists on aircraft with no tailplane at all
It is unrelated to the elevator or tailplane in any way

explanation: Because trimmed flight usually requires the tailplane (whether through a fixed elevator deflection, a trim tab, or an adjustable stabilizer) to produce a specific balancing force, that surface's own deflection or setting adds a small drag penalty on top of the aircraft's basic drag — the extra drag cost of staying in balance rather than flying perfectly clean.

question: Some modern aircraft, particularly certain fighters, are deliberately designed with "relaxed static stability" — meaning:

options.text: The aircraft is built with reduced, neutral, or even slightly negative natural static stability, relying on a fly-by-wire flight control computer to maintain control and stability artificially, in exchange for greater manoeuvrability
The aircraft has no flight controls at all
It refers only to aircraft that are statically unstable in roll, never in pitch
It means the aircraft cannot be trimmed

explanation: A naturally stable aircraft resists changing its flight condition, which works against rapid manoeuvring. By deliberately reducing (or even removing) natural static stability and having a fast-acting flight control computer provide artificial stability instead, a relaxed-stability design can be made far more manoeuvrable than natural aerodynamics alone would allow.

question: At high subsonic and transonic Mach numbers, an aircraft's neutral point tends to:

options.text: Shift aft, as compressibility and wing bending effects change the aerodynamic center's position, generally increasing static margin and stability at high speed
Shift forward, reducing stability at high speed
Remain in exactly the same position at any Mach number
Move only with changes in weight, never with speed

explanation: Compressibility effects and aeroelastic wing bending both tend to shift the aerodynamic center — and with it the neutral point — aft as Mach number increases through the high subsonic and transonic range, generally increasing static margin and longitudinal stability at high speed compared with low-speed flight, for the same center of gravity.

question: A conventional, low-mounted tailplane sitting within the wing's downwash typically has its stabilising contribution:

options.text: Somewhat reduced compared with an identical tailplane operating in clean, undisturbed air, since downwash reduces its effective angle of attack change per degree of aircraft pitch
Increased, since downwash always adds extra lift to the tailplane
Completely unaffected by downwash of any kind
Eliminated entirely by any amount of downwash

explanation: Downwash changes the local airflow direction the tailplane actually experiences, reducing how much its effective angle of attack changes for a given change in aircraft attitude compared with a tailplane in clean air — which somewhat reduces (without eliminating) its stabilising contribution, one reason the position of a low tailplane relative to the wing's wake is carefully considered in design.

question: As a wing approaches its stalling angle of attack, the downwash reaching a conventional tailplane can change abruptly, which can:

options.text: Produce a sudden change in the tailplane's effective angle of attack and pitching contribution right around the stall, distinct from the wing's own loss of lift
Have no effect on the tailplane whatsoever
Only affect the ailerons, never the tailplane
Always increase the tailplane's stabilising effect at the exact moment of the stall

explanation: The airflow pattern behind a wing changes significantly as it approaches and passes the stall, and the downwash reaching the tailplane can shift correspondingly — adding a further, sometimes abrupt, change in the tail's own pitching contribution right around the stall, on top of whatever the wing itself is doing.

question: Moving the center of gravity aft, within its approved range, generally reduces trim drag mainly because:

options.text: A shorter moment arm to the tailplane means less tailplane download is needed to balance the aircraft, reducing the drag that download itself produces
An aft CG always increases the tailplane download required
Trim drag is completely unrelated to CG position
Aft CG eliminates the need for a tailplane entirely

explanation: With the CG further aft, the wing's own nose-down pitching moment needs a smaller balancing download from the tailplane, since the moment arm involved has changed. That smaller required download itself produces less drag — one reason airlines pay close attention to managing CG toward the aft part of its approved range for fuel efficiency.

question: An aircraft's certified aft center of gravity limit is normally set somewhat ahead of the theoretical neutral point, rather than right at it, mainly to:

options.text: Provide a safety margin for CG measurement uncertainty, in-flight CG shift, and the difference between stick-fixed and stick-free stability, so a small error cannot push the aircraft into instability
Make the aircraft as unstable as legally possible
Match exactly the forward CG limit
Have no relationship to the neutral point at all

explanation: Because CG position is never known with perfect precision, can shift during flight, and stick-free stability can differ somewhat from stick-fixed, the certified aft limit is deliberately placed with a margin ahead of the theoretical neutral point — so ordinary uncertainty and in-flight variation cannot accidentally carry the aircraft into instability.

question: A classic flight test for static longitudinal stability involves:

options.text: Trimming for a target speed, then displacing the control column a known amount to change speed, releasing it, and observing whether the aircraft tends to return toward the trimmed speed
Measuring only the aircraft's maximum speed
Checking fuel flow at a fixed power setting
Observing the ailerons alone, with no reference to the elevator

explanation: A standard static stability check trims the aircraft at a chosen speed, then displaces it away from that trimmed speed with a control input before releasing the controls — a genuinely stable aircraft shows a clear, reasonable tendency to return toward the original trimmed speed on its own, which is exactly the initial-tendency definition static stability is built around.

question: The "manoeuvre point", distinct from the static neutral point, is the center of gravity position at which:

options.text: Stick-force-per-g in a manoeuvring (accelerated) condition falls to zero, accounting for pitch damping effects that the purely static neutral point does not include
The aircraft has exactly zero static stability in level, unaccelerated flight
The wing itself stalls
The two terms are simply different names for exactly the same CG position

explanation: The static neutral point is defined for steady, unaccelerated flight and does not account for the tailplane's pitch-damping contribution during a manoeuvre. The manoeuvre point extends the concept to accelerated (turning or pulling-g) flight, and is generally further aft than the static neutral point because pitch damping adds an extra stabilising effect once the aircraft is actually rotating.

question: Beyond providing a static restoring moment, the tailplane also contributes "pitch damping", meaning it:

options.text: Generates a moment that resists the rate of pitching itself, not just the aircraft's displacement from its trimmed attitude
Only resists displacement, never the rate of rotation
Has no relationship to pitch rate whatsoever
Amplifies any pitching motion once it begins

explanation: As the aircraft pitches, the tailplane's own velocity through the air (from the rotation itself) changes its local angle of attack in a way that opposes the rotation — a genuine damping moment resisting pitch rate, distinct from and additional to the static restoring moment that resists simple displacement from trim.

question: A classic swept-wing longitudinal stability problem, "pitch-up", occurs because at high angle of attack:

options.text: The wingtips (which are also further aft on a swept wing) tend to stall first, shifting the wing's overall center of lift forward and inboard, producing an additional nose-up pitching moment
The wing root always stalls before the tips on a swept wing
Pitch-up only affects unswept, rectangular wings
It has no relationship to which part of the wing stalls first

explanation: Because a swept wing's tips are both aft of the root and prone to stalling first, losing lift there shifts the wing's effective center of lift forward (and inboard), and that forward shift produces an additional nose-up pitching moment right when the aircraft is already at high angle of attack — a self-reinforcing tendency that swept-wing designs must specifically guard against.

question: A tailless flying-wing aircraft, with no separate horizontal tailplane, typically achieves longitudinal stability instead through:

options.text: A wing planform and aerofoil section (often with reflexed or twisted camber) shaped so the wing itself provides the needed restoring moment
An invisible tailplane with no physical structure
Relying entirely on engine thrust for pitch stability
It is aerodynamically impossible for a tailless aircraft to be stable

explanation: Without a separate tailplane to provide a stabilising moment, a flying wing must build the equivalent effect into the wing itself — commonly through washout and a reflexed (upward-curved) trailing edge or specific twist distribution — so the wing's own pitching moment characteristics provide the restoring tendency a conventional design gets from its tail.

question: Moving the center of gravity aft, within the approved range, tends to affect the phugoid oscillation by:

options.text: Changing its period and damping somewhat, generally in the direction of reduced damping as stability margin decreases
Having no effect on the phugoid at all
Eliminating the phugoid mode entirely
Only affecting the short-period mode, never the phugoid

explanation: Because the phugoid is bound up with the aircraft's overall longitudinal stability characteristics, moving the CG aft — and reducing static margin — tends to change the phugoid's period and generally reduce its damping, consistent with the aircraft's reduced overall resistance to a pitch/speed disturbance.

question: A heavier, more highly wing-loaded aircraft generally shows a short-period pitch response that is:

options.text: Slower, since greater mass and pitch inertia resist a rapid change in angle of attack more than a lighter, less loaded aircraft
Always faster than a lighter aircraft's
Completely unaffected by weight or wing loading
Only relevant to the phugoid, never the short-period mode

explanation: The short-period mode's frequency and response speed are influenced by the aircraft's pitch inertia as well as its aerodynamic damping. A heavier, more highly loaded aircraft generally has greater pitch inertia, giving it a slower, more sluggish short-period response than a lighter aircraft of similar aerodynamic design.

question: On a canard configuration, achieving positive longitudinal static stability generally requires the center of gravity to be positioned:

options.text: Ahead of the whole aircraft's neutral point, exactly the same underlying requirement as a conventional aft-tail design, even though the canard itself sits ahead of the wing
Behind the aircraft's neutral point
Exactly on top of the canard surface itself
Irrelevant to stability on a canard design

explanation: The fundamental static stability requirement — center of gravity ahead of the whole aircraft's neutral point — holds regardless of whether the stabilising surface sits ahead of or behind the wing; only the details of where that neutral point ends up, and how the canard and wing share the lift, differ between a canard and a conventional configuration.

question: A "stick pusher", fitted to some aircraft (particularly certain T-tail designs) as a stall protection device, works by:

options.text: Physically and forcefully moving the control column forward as angle of attack approaches a critical value, actively reducing angle of attack rather than merely warning the pilot
Only sounding an aural alert, with no physical control input
Permanently disabling the elevator once installed
Increasing the aircraft's critical angle of attack

explanation: Unlike a simple warning device, a stick pusher actively intervenes: as angle of attack approaches a dangerous value, it drives the control column forward with real, sometimes considerable force, physically reducing angle of attack before a full stall (or, on some T-tail designs, a deep stall) develops — a protection against configurations where a full stall could otherwise be difficult or impossible to recover from.

question: A "stick shaker" differs from a "stick pusher" in that the shaker:

options.text: Only vibrates the control column to warn the pilot of an approaching stall, without itself moving the column or changing angle of attack
Actively forces the control column forward, exactly like a pusher
Is only found on aircraft that also have a pusher, and never appears alone
Increases engine power automatically

explanation: A stick shaker is purely a warning device, vibrating the control column to alert the pilot to an approaching stall while leaving the actual flying entirely to them, whereas a stick pusher goes a step further and physically intervenes to reduce angle of attack — the two are often fitted together, with the shaker warning first and the pusher acting only if angle of attack continues increasing.

question: Beyond improving manoeuvrability, some modern transport aircraft are deliberately designed and operated toward the aft end of their CG range (a milder form of relaxed stability) mainly because:

options.text: A more aft CG reduces the tailplane download — and the trim drag that comes with it — needed for balanced flight, improving fuel efficiency
It has no effect on fuel efficiency at all
It always makes the aircraft impossible to trim
It only matters for fighter aircraft, never transport aircraft

explanation: Managing the CG toward the aft part of its approved range reduces the tailplane download needed to balance the aircraft, and with it the trim drag that download produces — a genuine fuel-efficiency motivation, distinct from (though related to) the manoeuvrability motivation behind fighter aircraft's much more aggressive relaxed-stability designs.
